answers: Search teams in Indonesia may have found the main fuselage of the AirAsia plane where most of the remaining victims and the plane's black boxes are expected to be. Authorities found "four big parts of the plane we're looking for," says the official in charge of the search in the Java Sea, reports Reuters. The biggest of the pieces is about 59 feet long and 18 feet wide, reports AP. The pieces have only been detected, not recovered, and divers hope conditions will permit them to reach the objects tomorrow. So far, only 30 of 162 bodies have been recovered, and most of the victims are believed to be still strapped in their seats. Authorities also said today that AirAsia was in violation of its license by flying to Singapore on a Sunday, the day of the crash, reports the Telegraph. As a result, the airline might have its license revoked in Indonesia. There's still no conclusions yet in what caused the crash, but theories continue to center on stormy conditions. "Flight 8501 appears to have been trapped in bad weather that would have been difficult to avoid," says a report by Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency.

full.prediction:
**Summary of AirAsia Flight 8501 Crash and Related Developments**

On December 28, 2014, AirAsia Flight 8501, an Airbus A320 carrying 162 passengers and crew, crashed into the Java Sea shortly after departing from Surabaya, Indonesia, en route to Singapore. The crash, which occurred during a monsoon season with intense tropical thunderstorms, resulted in no survivors. The search for the wreckage and victims has been ongoing, with significant developments reported over the following days.

Indonesian authorities confirmed that search teams had located four large parts of the plane on the sea bed, including a section measuring 18 meters long, believed to be part of the aircraft's fuselage. These findings were made using sonar equipment and underwater remote operating vehicles (ROVs), though poor visibility and strong currents have hindered detailed inspections. Divers, including Russian specialists, were expected to investigate the wreckage if weather conditions improved.

Despite the discovery of wreckage, the crucial black box recorders—flight data and cockpit voice recorders—have not yet been found. These devices are essential for determining the cause of the crash, which remains under investigation. The Indonesian Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency suggested that bad weather, including possible engine icing, may have contributed to the accident. The plane was flying at 32,000 feet and had requested to climb to 38,000 feet before losing contact with air traffic control.

The crash has also raised regulatory concerns. Indonesia's transport ministry stated that AirAsia had violated its operating license by flying the Surabaya to Singapore route on a Sunday, a day not permitted under its current schedule. As a result, the airline was suspended from operating this route, and a full review of all AirAsia flights in Indonesia was initiated. AirAsia, which is 49% owned by Malaysia-based AirAsia, has pledged to cooperate with the investigation.

Search efforts have involved a multi-national task force, including vessels and aircraft from Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, the U.S., and Russia. Over 60 vessels and 20 aircraft have been deployed to locate the wreckage and recover victims. As of the seventh day of the search, only 30 bodies had been recovered, with officials noting that the chances of finding more floating bodies were low. Some bodies were found on beaches, and others were recovered from the sea.

The crash has had a profound impact on the families
